title: Trummy Young in Honolulu and his influence on trombone playing
summary: In Honolulu, Trummy Young asks about the system; Maxwell calls Trummy the father of modern trombone playing.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Well, just a little follow-up on that, you remember the time we went to Honolulu for that jazz festival?

Tommy was very impressed with my chops. He said, man -- you know, he kept raving about my range and endurance and my age and everything. And I told him about my system and everything and he said he had false teeth. And he said, would you come over and show me some day? I said, Tommy, you never sounded better. You don't need any help. You sound better than you ever sounded and better than anybody else." But he said, he taught and he wanted to find out about it and everything.

I didn't know how well it would work on a trombone because it involves being able to push the valves down with one hand while you hold the mouthpiece with the other. And it would be hard on the trombone to get different positions.
But he worked something out so we spent an afternoon together. And he wrote me a nice letter and said, you know, he really -- he does the system everyday. So I feel sort of proud about him.

Oh, he's nice, he sure is. He was on that Mildred Bailey Show too, you know. He was always my favorite, next to Lawrence Brown. In fact, when we were in Honolulu I asked him, you know, I think, you know, like Trummy is the father of modern trombone playing in my opinion. Bill Harris and all these hotshot names and everything really got it from Trummy. And I used to get my head handed to me when I'd tell this to guys. "No, man." Et cetera.

So I told this to Trummy, I said, "How's it feel, you know, to have all these guys imitate you and everything?" He said, "I feel kind of complimented." I told him, "You know, you're really the father of modern trombone playing. I always believed Bill Harris copied you and everything." And I said, "I get my head handed to me for saying that." He said, "You know, that's true. Bill Harris told me so. He's a real nice guy and he always told me how much he appreciated, how much he'd gotten from me."
But I think that's true. That whole school of playing came out of Trummy Young.
